contents.title: The Pythagorean Theorem, Visually
contents.summary: Why a² + b² = c² is true — with a proof you can see — and how to use it to measure the world.
contents.author: Polymath Team

contents.body_html:
Every right triangle hides the same secret. Label the two short sides aa and bb, and the long side opposite the right angle — the hypotenuse — cc. Then:

a2+b2=c2a^2 + b^2 = c^2

It is one of the oldest results in mathematics, and you can see why it is true.

The picture proof

Take a big square with side length a+ba + b and place four copies of your triangle inside it, one in each corner. The space left in the middle is a tilted square whose side is cc.

Now count the area of the big square two different ways:

  1. As one big square: (a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2
  2. As four triangles plus the middle square: 4⋅12ab+c2=2ab+c24 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}ab + c^2 = 2ab + c^2

Both describe the same area, so

a2+2ab+b2=2ab+c2a2+b2=c2\begin{aligned} a^2 + 2ab + b^2 &= 2ab + c^2 \\ a^2 + b^2 &= c^2 \end{aligned}

Tip

Draw it yourself. Cut four paper triangles and slide them around inside the square — the proof clicks the moment you rearrange them.

Famous whole-number triangles

Some right triangles have whole-number sides. They are called Pythagorean triples:

a b c Check
3 4 5 9 + 16 = 25
5 12 13 25 + 144 = 169
8 15 17 64 + 225 = 289
7 24 25 49 + 576 = 625

Builders have used the 3-4-5 triangle for centuries to make perfect right angles with nothing but a knotted rope.

Using it: the ladder problem

A 5 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 3 m from the wall. How high up does it reach?

h=52−32=25−9=16=4 mh = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{25 - 9} = \sqrt{16} = 4\text{ m}

Bonus: distance between two points

The distance formula from coordinate geometry is the Pythagorean theorem in disguise. For points (x1,y1)(x_1, y_1) and (x2,y2)(x_2, y_2):

d=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}

Practice

  1. A TV screen is 48 inches wide and 27 inches tall. What is its diagonal?
  2. Is a triangle with sides 6, 8 and 11 a right triangle?

Answers: (1) 482+272=3033≈55.1\sqrt{48^2 + 27^2} = \sqrt{3033} \approx 55.1 inches. (2) No — 36+64=100≠12136 + 64 = 100 \ne 121.
contents.body_md:
Every right triangle hides the same secret. Label the two short sides $a$ and $b$, and the long side opposite the right angle — the **hypotenuse** — $c$. Then:

$$
a^2 + b^2 = c^2
$$

It is one of the oldest results in mathematics, and you can *see* why it is true.

<!-- more -->

## The picture proof

Take a big square with side length $a + b$ and place four copies of your triangle inside it, one in each corner. The space left in the middle is a tilted square whose side is $c$.

Now count the area of the big square two different ways:

1. As one big square: $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$
2. As four triangles plus the middle square: $4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}ab + c^2 = 2ab + c^2$

Both describe the same area, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^2 + 2ab + b^2 &= 2ab + c^2 \\
a^2 + b^2 &= c^2
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!TIP]
> Draw it yourself. Cut four paper triangles and slide them around inside the square — the proof clicks the moment you rearrange them.

## Famous whole-number triangles

Some right triangles have whole-number sides. They are called **Pythagorean triples**:

| a | b | c | Check |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 4 | 5 | 9 + 16 = 25 |
| 5 | 12 | 13 | 25 + 144 = 169 |
| 8 | 15 | 17 | 64 + 225 = 289 |
| 7 | 24 | 25 | 49 + 576 = 625 |

Builders have used the 3-4-5 triangle for centuries to make perfect right angles with nothing but a knotted rope.

## Using it: the ladder problem

A 5 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 3 m from the wall. How high up does it reach?

$$
h = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{25 - 9} = \sqrt{16} = 4\text{ m}
$$

## Bonus: distance between two points

The distance formula from coordinate geometry *is* the Pythagorean theorem in disguise. For points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$:

$$
d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}
$$

## Practice

1. A TV screen is 48 inches wide and 27 inches tall. What is its diagonal?
2. Is a triangle with sides 6, 8 and 11 a right triangle?

**Answers:** (1) $\sqrt{48^2 + 27^2} = \sqrt{3033} \approx 55.1$ inches. (2) No — $36 + 64 = 100 \ne 121$.

contents.title: Multiply Any Two-Digit Number by 11 in Your Head
contents.summary: A two-second trick that makes you look like a human calculator.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html:
To multiply a two-digit number by 11, split its digits apart and put their sum in the middle.

36×11  →  3 (3+6)‾ 6=39636 \times 11 \;\to\; 3\,\underline{(3+6)}\,6 = 396

headings.text: When the sum is 10 or more

contents.body_html:
To multiply a two-digit number by 11, split its digits apart and put their sum in the middle.

36×11  →  3 (3+6)‾ 6=39636 \times 11 \;\to\; 3\,\underline{(3+6)}\,6 = 396

When the sum is 10 or more

Carry the 1 into the first digit:

78×11  →  7 (7+8)‾ 8=7 15‾ 8  →  85878 \times 11 \;\to\; 7\,\underline{(7+8)}\,8 = 7\,\underline{15}\,8 \;\to\; 858

Why it works

11×n=10n+n11 \times n = 10n + n. Writing n=10a+bn = 10a + b:

11(10a+b)=100a+10(a+b)+b11(10a + b) = 100a + 10(a + b) + b

The hundreds digit is aa, the tens digit is a+ba + b and the ones digit is bb — exactly the trick.

Tip

Try these: 45 × 11, 62 × 11, 99 × 11. (Answers: 495, 682, 1089.)
contents.body_md:
To multiply a two-digit number by 11, **split its digits apart and put their sum in the middle**.

$$
36 \times 11 \;\to\; 3\,\underline{(3+6)}\,6 = 396
$$

<!-- more -->

## When the sum is 10 or more

Carry the 1 into the first digit:

$$
78 \times 11 \;\to\; 7\,\underline{(7+8)}\,8 = 7\,\underline{15}\,8 \;\to\; 858
$$

## Why it works

$11 \times n = 10n + n$. Writing $n = 10a + b$:

$$
11(10a + b) = 100a + 10(a + b) + b
$$

The hundreds digit is $a$, the tens digit is $a + b$ and the ones digit is $b$ — exactly the trick.

> [!TIP]
> Try these: 45 × 11, 62 × 11, 99 × 11. (Answers: 495, 682, 1089.)

contents.title: Calculus in a Weekend
contents.summary: Limits, derivatives and integrals explained with intuition first — a complete short course in five chapters.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: Calculus is the mathematics of change. Speed is the change in distance; acceleration is the change in speed; the area under a curve adds up infinitely many tiny changes. This short ebook gives you the core ideas in a weekend — intuition first, formulas second.
contents.body_html:
Calculus is the mathematics of change. Speed is the change in distance; acceleration is the change in speed; the area under a curve adds up infinitely many tiny changes. This short ebook gives you the core ideas in a weekend — intuition first, formulas second.

Chapter 1 · Limits

A limit asks: what value does f(x)f(x) approach as xx gets closer and closer to some number? We write

lim⁡x→af(x)=L\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L

The function does not even need to be defined at aa. A classic example:

lim⁡x→0sin⁡xx=1\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1

Plug in x=0x = 0 and you get 00\tfrac{0}{0}, which is meaningless — yet values like x=0.01x = 0.01 give 0.99998…0.99998\ldots. The limit captures where the function is heading.

Note

Limits are the foundation everything else is built on. If a definition later looks scary, look for the limit hiding inside it.

Chapter 2 · Derivatives

The derivative measures instantaneous rate of change — the slope of the curve at a single point:

f′(x)=lim⁡h→0f(x+h)−f(x)hf'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}

You rarely compute it from the definition. A handful of rules cover most cases:

Rule Formula
Power ddxxn=nxn−1\dfrac{d}{dx} x^n = n x^{n-1}
Sum (f+g)′=f′+g′(f + g)' = f' + g'
Product (fg)′=f′g+fg′(fg)' = f'g + fg'
Chain ddxf(g(x))=f′(g(x)) g′(x)\dfrac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))\, g'(x)

Example. If a ball’s height is h(t)=20t−5t2h(t) = 20t - 5t^2 metres, its velocity is h′(t)=20−10th'(t) = 20 - 10t. It stops rising when h′(t)=0h'(t) = 0, at t=2t = 2 seconds, reaching h(2)=20h(2) = 20 metres.

Chapter 3 · Integrals

An integral adds up infinitely many infinitely thin slices. The definite integral is the signed area under a curve:

∫abf(x) dx\int_a^b f(x)\,dx

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus connects integrals to derivatives: if F′(x)=f(x)F'(x) = f(x), then

∫abf(x) dx=F(b)−F(a)\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)

Example. The area under y=x2y = x^2 from 0 to 3:

∫03x2 dx=[x33]03=273−0=9\int_0^3 x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = \frac{27}{3} - 0 = 9

Chapter 4 · Applications

Optimization. You have 20 m of fence and want the largest rectangular pen. With width xx, the length is 10−x10 - x and the area is

A(x)=x(10−x)=10x−x2,A′(x)=10−2xA(x) = x(10 - x) = 10x - x^2, \qquad A'(x) = 10 - 2x

Setting A′(x)=0A'(x) = 0 gives x=5x = 5: a 5×55 \times 5 square with area 25 m225\text{ m}^2.

Motion. Integrate velocity to get distance travelled; differentiate position to get velocity. The two operations undo each other.

Chapter 5 · Where to go next

  • Practise derivatives until the rules are automatic.
  • Learn u-substitution and integration by parts — the integral versions of the chain and product rules.
  • Explore differential equations, which describe everything from population growth to circuits.

Tip

Fifteen minutes a day beats a three-hour cram. Calculus rewards repetition.
contents.body_md:
Calculus is the mathematics of change. Speed is the change in distance; acceleration is the change in speed; the area under a curve adds up infinitely many tiny changes. This short ebook gives you the core ideas in a weekend — intuition first, formulas second.

<!-- more -->

## Chapter 1 · Limits

A **limit** asks: *what value does $f(x)$ approach as $x$ gets closer and closer to some number?* We write

$$
\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L
$$

The function does not even need to be defined at $a$. A classic example:

$$
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1
$$

Plug in $x = 0$ and you get $\tfrac{0}{0}$, which is meaningless — yet values like $x = 0.01$ give $0.99998\ldots$. The limit captures where the function is *heading*.

> [!NOTE]
> Limits are the foundation everything else is built on. If a definition later looks scary, look for the limit hiding inside it.

## Chapter 2 · Derivatives

The **derivative** measures instantaneous rate of change — the slope of the curve at a single point:

$$
f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}
$$

You rarely compute it from the definition. A handful of rules cover most cases:

| Rule | Formula |
|---|---|
| Power | $\dfrac{d}{dx} x^n = n x^{n-1}$ |
| Sum | $(f + g)' = f' + g'$ |
| Product | $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$ |
| Chain | $\dfrac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))\, g'(x)$ |

**Example.** If a ball's height is $h(t) = 20t - 5t^2$ metres, its velocity is $h'(t) = 20 - 10t$. It stops rising when $h'(t) = 0$, at $t = 2$ seconds, reaching $h(2) = 20$ metres.

## Chapter 3 · Integrals

An **integral** adds up infinitely many infinitely thin slices. The definite integral is the signed area under a curve:

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
$$

The **Fundamental Theorem of Calculus** connects integrals to derivatives: if $F'(x) = f(x)$, then

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)
$$

**Example.** The area under $y = x^2$ from 0 to 3:

$$
\int_0^3 x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = \frac{27}{3} - 0 = 9
$$

## Chapter 4 · Applications

**Optimization.** You have 20 m of fence and want the largest rectangular pen. With width $x$, the length is $10 - x$ and the area is

$$
A(x) = x(10 - x) = 10x - x^2, \qquad A'(x) = 10 - 2x
$$

Setting $A'(x) = 0$ gives $x = 5$: a $5 \times 5$ square with area $25\text{ m}^2$.

**Motion.** Integrate velocity to get distance travelled; differentiate position to get velocity. The two operations undo each other.

## Chapter 5 · Where to go next

- Practise derivatives until the rules are automatic.
- Learn **u-substitution** and **integration by parts** — the integral versions of the chain and product rules.
- Explore **differential equations**, which describe everything from population growth to circuits.

> [!TIP]
> Fifteen minutes a day beats a three-hour cram. Calculus rewards repetition.

contents.title: Read Sheet Music in 10 Minutes
contents.summary: Staff, clefs, note names and rhythm — everything you need to read your first melody today.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: Sheet music looks intimidating, but it answers just two questions: which note (up and down) and how long (left to right). Here is the melody you will be able to read by the end of this lesson:

headings.text: 1. The staff and the treble clef
2. Rhythm: how long each note lasts

contents.body_html:
Sheet music looks intimidating, but it answers just two questions: which note (up and down) and how long (left to right). Here is the melody you will be able to read by the end of this lesson:

1. The staff and the treble clef

Music is written on a staff of five lines. The swirly treble clef at the start wraps around the second line from the bottom, marking it as the note G.

  • Notes on the lines, bottom to top: E G B D F — “Every Good Boy Does Fine”.
  • Notes in the spaces, bottom to top: F A C E — it spells face.

Middle C sits on its own short line (a ledger line) just below the staff.

2. Rhythm: how long each note lasts

In the most common time signature, 4/4, each bar holds four beats:

Note Beats in 4/4
Whole note (hollow, no stem) 4
Half note (hollow, with stem) 2
Quarter note (filled, with stem) 1
Eighth note (filled, with a flag) ½

The top number of the time signature says how many beats are in a bar; the bottom number says which note gets one beat (4 = quarter note).

3. Read the melody

Go back to Twinkle, Twinkle above and read it bar by bar:

  1. C C G G — four quarter notes
  2. A A G — two quarters, then a half note held for two beats
  3. F F E E
  4. D D C — ending on a half note

Tip

Clap the rhythm first, then say the note names, and only then play. Separating the two skills makes both easier.

4. A scale to practise

The C major scale uses only the white keys of a piano:

Read it once a day this week and note-reading will start to feel automatic.

## 1. The staff and the treble clef

Music is written on a **staff** of five lines. The swirly **treble clef** at the start wraps around the second line from the bottom, marking it as the note **G**.

- Notes on the **lines**, bottom to top: **E G B D F** — "Every Good Boy Does Fine".
- Notes in the **spaces**, bottom to top: **F A C E** — it spells *face*.

Middle C sits on its own short line (a *ledger line*) just below the staff.

## 2. Rhythm: how long each note lasts

In the most common time signature, **4/4**, each bar holds four beats:

| Note | Beats in 4/4 |
|---|---|
| Whole note (hollow, no stem) | 4 |
| Half note (hollow, with stem) | 2 |
| Quarter note (filled, with stem) | 1 |
| Eighth note (filled, with a flag) | ½ |

The top number of the time signature says how many beats are in a bar; the bottom number says which note gets one beat (4 = quarter note).

## 3. Read the melody

Go back to *Twinkle, Twinkle* above and read it bar by bar:

1. C C G G — four quarter notes
2. A A G — two quarters, then a **half note** held for two beats
3. F F E E
4. D D C — ending on a half note

> [!TIP]
> Clap the rhythm first, then say the note names, and only then play. Separating the two skills makes both easier.

## 4. A scale to practise

The C major scale uses only the white keys of a piano:

```abc
X:2
T:C major scale
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C D E F | G A B c | c B A G | F E D C |]
```

Read it once a day this week and note-reading will start to feel automatic.

contents.title: The Circle of Fifths, Explained
contents.summary: The single diagram that explains key signatures, relative minors and why some chords just sound right together.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: The circle of fifths arranges all twelve major keys so that each step clockwise moves up a perfect fifth — and adds exactly one sharp to the key signature. Once you understand it, key signatures stop being something to memorise.

headings.text: Why neighbouring keys sound good together

contents.body_html:
The circle of fifths arranges all twelve major keys so that each step clockwise moves up a perfect fifth — and adds exactly one sharp to the key signature. Once you understand it, key signatures stop being something to memorise.

Going clockwise: sharps

Start at C major (no sharps or flats) at the top. Each clockwise step goes up a fifth:

Key Sharps
C 0
G 1 — F♯
D 2 — F♯ C♯
A 3 — F♯ C♯ G♯
E 4
B 5
F♯ 6
C♯ 7

Sharps are always added in the same order: F C G D A E B — “Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle”.

Going anticlockwise: flats

Moving the other way goes down a fifth and adds a flat each time: F (1♭), B♭ (2), E♭ (3), A♭ (4), D♭ (5), G♭ (6), C♭ (7).

Flats appear in the reverse order: B E A D G C F — “Battle Ends And Down Goes Charles’ Father”.

Relative minors

Every major key shares its key signature with a relative minor, found three semitones below it: C major ↔ A minor, G major ↔ E minor, F major ↔ D minor. On most diagrams these sit on an inner ring.

Why neighbouring keys sound good together

Keys next to each other on the circle share six of their seven notes. That is why the chords built on neighbouring keys — I, IV and V — form the backbone of countless songs. Here is the famous I–V–vi–IV progression in C major:

Tip

To find the I, IV and V chords of any key, look at the key on the circle and its two neighbours: the one anticlockwise is IV, the one clockwise is V.

Practise it

  1. How many sharps does A major have? (3)
  2. What is the relative minor of E♭ major? (C minor)
  3. Which chords are I, IV and V in G major? (G, C, D)

The circle of fifths arranges all twelve major keys so that each step clockwise moves up a **perfect fifth** — and adds exactly one sharp to the key signature. Once you understand it, key signatures stop being something to memorise.

<!-- more -->

## Going clockwise: sharps

Start at **C major** (no sharps or flats) at the top. Each clockwise step goes up a fifth:

| Key | Sharps |
|---|---|
| C | 0 |
| G | 1 — F♯ |
| D | 2 — F♯ C♯ |
| A | 3 — F♯ C♯ G♯ |
| E | 4 |
| B | 5 |
| F♯ | 6 |
| C♯ | 7 |

Sharps are always added in the same order: **F C G D A E B** — "Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle".

## Going anticlockwise: flats

Moving the other way goes *down* a fifth and adds a flat each time: **F** (1♭), **B♭** (2), **E♭** (3), **A♭** (4), **D♭** (5), **G♭** (6), **C♭** (7).

Flats appear in the reverse order: **B E A D G C F** — "Battle Ends And Down Goes Charles' Father".

## Relative minors

Every major key shares its key signature with a **relative minor**, found three semitones below it: C major ↔ A minor, G major ↔ E minor, F major ↔ D minor. On most diagrams these sit on an inner ring.

## Why neighbouring keys sound good together

Keys next to each other on the circle share six of their seven notes. That is why the chords built on neighbouring keys — I, IV and V — form the backbone of countless songs. Here is the famous **I–V–vi–IV** progression in C major:

```abc
X:1
T:I–V–vi–IV in C major
M:4/4
L:1/2
K:C
"C"[CEG]2 | "G"[B,DG]2 | "Am"[A,CE]2 | "F"[A,CF]2 |]
```

> [!TIP]
> To find the I, IV and V chords of any key, look at the key on the circle and its two neighbours: the one anticlockwise is IV, the one clockwise is V.

## Practise it

1. How many sharps does **A major** have? *(3)*
2. What is the relative minor of **E♭ major**? *(C minor)*
3. Which chords are I, IV and V in **G major**? *(G, C, D)*

contents.title: The 60% Metronome Rule
contents.summary: Practise slowly on purpose and you will reach full speed faster. Here's the exact routine.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: Mistakes you repeat at full speed become habits. Slow, perfect repetitions build accuracy that survives when you speed up.
contents.body_html:
Mistakes you repeat at full speed become habits. Slow, perfect repetitions build accuracy that survives when you speed up.

The routine

  1. Find your target tempo — say 120 BPM.
  2. Set the metronome to 60% of it: 120×0.6=72120 \times 0.6 = 72 BPM.
  3. Play the passage three times in a row with no mistakes.
  4. Raise the tempo by 4–5 BPM and repeat.
  5. If you make a mistake twice, drop back one step.

Tip

Stop for the day when you reach a tempo you can’t play cleanly three times. Your brain consolidates the skill overnight — tomorrow’s starting point will be higher.

It feels slow. It is slow. And it is the fastest way to play fast.

contents.title: Python for Absolute Beginners
contents.summary: Go from zero to writing real programs. Six short chapters, plenty of examples and a mini project.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: Python reads almost like English, runs everywhere, and powers everything from websites to data science and AI. This ebook takes you from your very first line of code to a small program you build yourself.
contents.body_html:
Python reads almost like English, runs everywhere, and powers everything from websites to data science and AI. This ebook takes you from your very first line of code to a small program you build yourself.

Chapter 1 · Setting up

Install Python 3 from python.org (on macOS and Linux it is often already installed). Open a terminal and start the interactive interpreter:

python3

Type your first line of code and press Enter:

print("Hello, world!")

Tip

The interpreter is a calculator too. Try 2 ** 10 or 7 / 2.

Chapter 2 · Variables and types

A variable is a name for a value:

name = "Ada"          # str  — text
age = 36              # int  — whole number
height = 1.65         # float — decimal number
is_learning = True    # bool — True or False

print(f"{name} is {age} years old")

The f before the quotes makes an f-string: anything inside {} is evaluated and inserted.

Chapter 3 · Making decisions and repeating

temperature = 23

if temperature > 30:
    print("Hot!")
elif temperature > 15:
    print("Pleasant.")
else:
    print("Bring a jacket.")

for i in range(3):
    print("Lap", i + 1)

count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1
print("Lift-off!")

Indentation matters in Python: the indented lines belong to the if, for or while above them.

Chapter 4 · Functions

Functions package up code you want to reuse:

def area_of_circle(radius: float) -> float:
    """Return the area of a circle."""
    return 3.14159 * radius ** 2

print(area_of_circle(2))   # 12.56636

Chapter 5 · Lists and dictionaries

scores = [72, 95, 88]
scores.append(100)
print(max(scores), sum(scores) / len(scores))   # 100 88.75

capitals = {"France": "Paris", "Japan": "Tokyo"}
capitals["Kenya"] = "Nairobi"
for country, city in capitals.items():
    print(f"The capital of {country} is {city}")

Chapter 6 · Mini project: word counter

Python reads almost like English, runs everywhere, and powers everything from websites to data science and AI. This ebook takes you from your very first line of code to a small program you build yourself.

<!-- more -->

## Chapter 1 · Setting up

Install Python 3 from python.org (on macOS and Linux it is often already installed). Open a terminal and start the interactive interpreter:

```bash
python3
```

Type your first line of code and press Enter:

```python
print("Hello, world!")
```

> [!TIP]
> The interpreter is a calculator too. Try `2 ** 10` or `7 / 2`.

## Chapter 2 · Variables and types

A **variable** is a name for a value:

```python
name = "Ada"          # str  — text
age = 36              # int  — whole number
height = 1.65         # float — decimal number
is_learning = True    # bool — True or False

print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
```

The `f` before the quotes makes an **f-string**: anything inside `{}` is evaluated and inserted.

## Chapter 3 · Making decisions and repeating

```python
temperature = 23

if temperature > 30:
    print("Hot!")
elif temperature > 15:
    print("Pleasant.")
else:
    print("Bring a jacket.")

for i in range(3):
    print("Lap", i + 1)

count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1
print("Lift-off!")
```

Indentation matters in Python: the indented lines belong to the `if`, `for` or `while` above them.

## Chapter 4 · Functions

Functions package up code you want to reuse:

```python
def area_of_circle(radius: float) -> float:
    """Return the area of a circle."""
    return 3.14159 * radius ** 2

print(area_of_circle(2))   # 12.56636
```

## Chapter 5 · Lists and dictionaries

```python
scores = [72, 95, 88]
scores.append(100)
print(max(scores), sum(scores) / len(scores))   # 100 88.75

capitals = {"France": "Paris", "Japan": "Tokyo"}
capitals["Kenya"] = "Nairobi"
for country, city in capitals.items():
    print(f"The capital of {country} is {city}")
```

contents.title: Big-O Notation Without the Jargon
contents.summary: How to tell whether your code will still be fast when the data gets big — explained with everyday examples.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: Big-O notation describes how the work an algorithm does grows as its input grows. It ignores the details and asks one question: if the data gets ten times bigger, how much slower does this get?

headings.text: The fix is often a better data structure

contents.body_html:
Big-O notation describes how the work an algorithm does grows as its input grows. It ignores the details and asks one question: if the data gets ten times bigger, how much slower does this get?

The common growth rates

Big-O Name Everyday example
O(1)O(1) constant Looking up a word by page number
O(log⁡n)O(\log n) logarithmic Finding a name in a phone book by halving
O(n)O(n) linear Reading every page of a book
O(nlog⁡n)O(n \log n) linearithmic Sorting a deck of cards efficiently
O(n2)O(n^2) quadratic Comparing every person in a room with everyone else

Seeing it in code

// O(1): one step, no matter how long the array is
const first = (items) => items[0];

// O(n): looks at every item once
function contains(items, target) {
  for (const item of items) {
    if (item === target) return true;
  }
  return false;
}

// O(n²): compares every pair
function hasDuplicate(items) {
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    for (let j = i + 1; j < items.length; j++) {
      if (items[i] === items[j]) return true;
    }
  }
  return false;
}

The quadratic version makes n(n−1)2\frac{n(n-1)}{2} comparisons. For 1,000 items that is about half a million; for 1,000,000 items, half a trillion.

The fix is often a better data structure

// O(n): a Set remembers what we've seen
function hasDuplicateFast(items) {
  const seen = new Set();
  for (const item of items) {
    if (seen.has(item)) return true;
    seen.add(item);
  }
  return false;
}

Tip

When code feels slow, look for a loop inside a loop. A Set or a Map can often turn O(n2)O(n^2) into O(n)O(n).

Why logarithms are magic

Binary search halves the remaining data at every step, so a sorted list of a billion items takes at most about 30 steps, because 230≈1.07×1092^{30} \approx 1.07 \times 10^9.

contents.title: Git: Undo (Almost) Anything
contents.summary: The six commands that rescue you from the most common Git mistakes.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: Made a mess in Git? Find your situation below.
contents.body_html:
Made a mess in Git? Find your situation below.

Discard changes to a file you haven’t staged

git restore path/to/file

Unstage a file (keep the changes)

git restore --staged path/to/file

Fix the last commit message, or add a forgotten file

git add forgotten-file
git commit --amend

Undo the last commit but keep its changes

git reset --soft HEAD~1

Undo a commit that is already pushed (creates a new commit that reverses it)

git revert <commit-sha>

Recover “lost” work

git reflog          # find the commit you were on
git switch -c rescue <sha>

Warning

Never reset or --amend commits you have already pushed to a shared branch — use revert instead.
contents.body_md:
Made a mess in Git? Find your situation below.

<!-- more -->

**Discard changes to a file you haven't staged**

```bash
git restore path/to/file
```

**Unstage a file (keep the changes)**

```bash
git restore --staged path/to/file
```

**Fix the last commit message, or add a forgotten file**

```bash
git add forgotten-file
git commit --amend
```

**Undo the last commit but keep its changes**

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1
```

**Undo a commit that is already pushed** (creates a new commit that reverses it)

```bash
git revert <commit-sha>
```

**Recover "lost" work**

```bash
git reflog          # find the commit you were on
git switch -c rescue <sha>
```

> [!WARNING]
> Never `reset` or `--amend` commits you have already pushed to a shared branch — use `revert` instead.

contents.title: Build a REST API with Node.js and TypeScript
contents.summary: Design, build and test a small JSON API for a to-do app — routes, validation and error handling included.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: In this tutorial you will build a small but real JSON API for a to-do list using Node.js, Express and TypeScript, and learn the conventions that make APIs pleasant to use.
contents.body_html:
In this tutorial you will build a small but real JSON API for a to-do list using Node.js, Express and TypeScript, and learn the conventions that make APIs pleasant to use.

1. Set up the project

mkdir todo-api && cd todo-api
npm init -y
npm install express
npm install -D typescript tsx @types/express @types/node
npx tsc --init

2. Design the routes first

Method Path Meaning
GET /todos List all to-dos
POST /todos Create a to-do
PATCH /todos/:id Update a to-do
DELETE /todos/:id Delete a to-do

Nouns in the path, verbs in the HTTP method — that is the heart of REST.

3. Write the server

import express, { type Request, type Response } from 'express';

interface Todo {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  done: boolean;
}

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

let todos: Todo[] = [];
let nextId = 1;

app.get('/todos', (_req: Request, res: Response) => {
  res.json(todos);
});

app.post('/todos', (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const title = String(req.body?.title ?? '').trim();
  if (!title) {
    res.status(400).json({ error: 'title is required' });
    return;
  }
  const todo: Todo = { id: nextId++, title, done: false };
  todos.push(todo);
  res.status(201).json(todo);
});

app.patch('/todos/:id', (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const todo = todos.find((t) => t.id === Number(req.params.id));
  if (!todo) {
    res.status(404).json({ error: 'not found' });
    return;
  }
  if (typeof req.body?.done === 'boolean') todo.done = req.body.done;
  if (typeof req.body?.title === 'string') todo.title = req.body.title.trim();
  res.json(todo);
});

app.delete('/todos/:id', (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const before = todos.length;
  todos = todos.filter((t) => t.id !== Number(req.params.id));
  res.status(todos.length < before ? 204 : 404).end();
});

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('API running on http://localhost:3000'));

Run it with npx tsx server.ts.

4. Try it

curl -X POST localhost:3000/todos -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Learn REST"}'
curl localhost:3000/todos
curl -X PATCH localhost:3000/todos/1 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"done":true}'

5. Status codes that matter

  • 200 OK — here is what you asked for
  • 201 Created — returned after a successful POST
  • 204 No Content — success with nothing to return (deletes)
  • 400 Bad Request — the client sent invalid data
  • 404 Not Found — no such resource

Tip

Next, swap the in-memory array for a real database and add automated tests — the routes won’t need to change at all.

contents.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
contents.summary: Sunlight, tiny air molecules and one surprisingly steep formula explain blue skies and red sunsets.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: Sunlight looks white, but it is a mix of every colour of the rainbow. On its way through the atmosphere it bumps into nitrogen and oxygen molecules that are far smaller than the wavelength of light — and that is where the blue comes from.

headings.text: Then why isn’t the sky violet?

contents.body_html:
Sunlight looks white, but it is a mix of every colour of the rainbow. On its way through the atmosphere it bumps into nitrogen and oxygen molecules that are far smaller than the wavelength of light — and that is where the blue comes from.

Rayleigh scattering

Small particles scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones. The amount of scattering is proportional to one over the wavelength to the fourth power:

I∝1λ4I \propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}

Blue light (about 450 nm) versus red light (about 700 nm):

(700450)4≈5.9\left(\frac{700}{450}\right)^4 \approx 5.9

So blue light is scattered roughly six times more than red. Wherever you look in the sky, scattered blue light is coming towards you.

Then why isn’t the sky violet?

Violet light has an even shorter wavelength, but:

  • the Sun emits less violet than blue,
  • some violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and
  • our eyes are much more sensitive to blue.

Red sunsets

At sunset, light travels through far more air to reach you. Most of the blue is scattered away along the path, leaving the oranges and reds.

Note

On Mars the effect is reversed: fine dust makes the daytime sky butterscotch and sunsets bluish.

contents.title: Spaced Repetition: Remember New Words for Good
contents.summary: Review words just before you forget them and you'll need a fraction of the study time.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus showed that we forget new information on a predictable curve — fast at first, then more slowly. Each time you successfully recall something, the curve flattens and you remember it for longer.
contents.body_html:
In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus showed that we forget new information on a predictable curve — fast at first, then more slowly. Each time you successfully recall something, the curve flattens and you remember it for longer.

The idea

Instead of cramming a word ten times today, review it a few times spread out, each gap longer than the last.

Review When
1 Same day
2 1 day later
3 3 days later
4 1 week later
5 2 weeks later
6 1 month later

The Leitner box (no app needed)

  1. Write each word on a card and put new cards in Box 1.
  2. Review Box 1 daily, Box 2 every 3 days, Box 3 weekly.
  3. Remember the word? Move the card up a box.
  4. Forget it? It goes back to Box 1.

Tip

Put the word in a sentence on the back of the card. Words learned in context stick far better than isolated translations.

Ten minutes a day of spaced review beats an hour of cramming once a week.

contents.title: The Pomodoro Technique, Done Right
contents.summary: Twenty-five minutes of focus, five minutes of rest — plus the details most people skip.
contents.author: Polymath Team
contents.preview_html: The Pomodoro Technique, created by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s, breaks work into short, focused intervals separated by breaks.

headings.text: The details that make it work

contents.body_html:
The Pomodoro Technique, created by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s, breaks work into short, focused intervals separated by breaks.

The basic cycle

  1. Pick one task.
  2. Set a timer for 25 minutes and work on nothing else.
  3. Take a 5-minute break — stand up, stretch, look away from screens.
  4. After four rounds, take a longer 15–30 minute break.

The details that make it work

  • Write distractions down instead of acting on them. Deal with the list during breaks.
  • Plan your pomodoros at the start of the day; estimating builds a sense of how long things really take.
  • Protect the break. Scrolling your phone is not rest.

Tip

If 25 minutes feels too short for deep work like coding or composing, try 50/10. The principle — focused sprints with real breaks — matters more than the exact numbers.
